title: Where Most CPD Goes Wrong, Priorities and Timescales
author: Adam Robbins
summary: Adam Robbins argues that most CPD fails to produce lasting change because schools chase too many priorities at once and abandon initiatives before they take hold. He proposes four fixes: do less CPD by planning improvement over multiple years rather than a single year's list; prioritise a genuine single focus rather than the illusion of three priorities; establish specific, measurable success criteria so leaders know when to move on; and lean into a single school-wide focus rather than differentiating CPD by individual teacher need, on the theory that a shared, high-profile target builds stronger peer support and faster habit formation. He frames this as essential to both student outcomes and teacher retention.
points: Robbins's central diagnosis: 'Most CPD will not stick. Most schools move on from things too fast and end up back at square one' -- a claim that went viral on his own feed with little pushback despite his obvious 'skin in the game' as a CPD provider.

He argues genuine prioritisation means having exactly one priority at a time, not three, because schools with three priorities are really pursuing generic, siloed technique lists rather than a coherent model of great teaching.

He insists on measurable success criteria (e.g., 'in a review of cold call, 95% of lessons show habitual use') rather than vague goals like 'embedded and seen regularly,' so leaders know precisely when to move to the next priority.
He argues a single, school-wide CPD focus builds stronger peer support and faster habit change through 'complex contagion' across a staff network, compared to individualised differentiation.
quotes: I think it's pretty depressing but important to say: Most CPD will not stick. Most schools move on from things too fast and end up back at square one.
The two most important ingredients for teacher improvement are persistence and patience.
Prioritising is having one priority. This thing is the one thing we must get right first. This is our foundation, our bedrock of improvement that everything else will grow from.
If we establish a criteria that is more specific like 'In a review of cold call 95% of lessons show habitual use' then we now have a measurable target.
By doing less and being patient we can create meaningful change in the teachers in our schools and create a culture of continuous improvement.
